property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender breaks this by leaving owner equal to the caller for some newOwner inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead of newOwner will cause owner() != newOwner for some fuzzed newOwner inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() becomes exactly the provided newOwner (the buggy mutant sets owner to msg.sender, which will differ when newOwner != msg.sender).

For any caller who is the contract's current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets owner() to newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender instead will leave owner() as the caller for many newOwner inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any nonzero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always updates C.owner() to newOwner in the reference; the mutant that deletes the assignment fails to update owner for some inputs.

For any owner-address currentOwner and any candidate newOwner != currentOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) from currentOwner updates C.owner() to equal newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment breaks this by leaving owner unchanged for some newOwner values.

For any addresses currentOwner and newOwner, if currentOwner calls transferOwnership(newOwner) then C.owner() equals newOwner afterwards; the mutant that removes the assignment can leave owner unchanged for some newOwner inputs.

For any addresses originalOwner and candidateNewOwner where originalOwner is the current owner and candidateNewOwner is any address (including equal or zero), after originalOwner calls transferOwnership(candidateNewOwner) the contract's owner() equals candidateNewOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment can leave owner() unchanged for some candidateNewOwner values, so the property detects that difference.

For any address newOwner and when msg.sender equals the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets C.owner() to newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment can leave owner unchanged for some newOwner inputs.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), allowing owner to change and thus breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller that is the contract owner, calling owned() does not change the owner (reference keeps owner unchanged; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() which can change owner when msg.sender != owner in some scenarios).

For every caller, invoking owned() does not change the contract's owner (the reference preserves owner across the call; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so when a non-owner successfully calls owned() under some set-up the owner can change).

For any address that is allowed to call owned() (i.e., the current owner), invoking owned() does not change the contract's owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), which can change owner when a different address becomes owner before the call and then calls owned() (e.g., via a call originating from a contract whose msg.sender is that contract), breaking the invariant.

For every external caller address, a successful call to owned() does not change C.owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned(), so it can mutate owner for some caller addresses and thus violate this invariant.

For any caller who is the contract owner, invoking owned() does not change the owner (owner remains equal to the caller); the mutant violates this by setting owner to address(0) inside owned(), so after the call owner != caller for some input.

For any caller who is the contract owner, calling owned() preserves owner (owner remains equal to msg.sender); the mutant breaks this by setting owner to address(0) inside owned(), so after a successful call owner != caller for some owner addresses.

For any address that is the contract owner, calling owned() does not change the stored owner (owner remains equal to msg.sender); the mutant sets owner to address(0) inside owned(), breaking this rule for owner addresses.

For every caller that is NOT the contract owner, calling owned() must revert (onlyOwner), so the call never executes and owner remains unchanged; the mutant does not change this behavior for non-owners but does change behavior for owner — to make a universal property that holds for reference but is broken by mutant, we require that whenever owned() call succeeds, the owner after the call is equal to the address returned by tx.origin (which for the correct contract equals msg.sender when called directly) — we instead use a helper attacker contract that calls C.owned() so msg.sender != tx.origin; in the reference C this call will revert because only the owner can call owned(), so any non-owner caller (the helper) will fail and the call will not succeed; thus for all helper addresses the call to owned() should revert (ok==false); the mutant (which sets owner = address(0)) still requires onlyOwner and so also reverts for non-owner, so to distinguish we instead fuzz an owner address and ensure that when the owner calls owned() successfully the owner remains unchanged — the reference preserves owner==caller after owned(), but the mutant sets owner to address(0) thus failing. (Test uses fuzzed owner address that we set as owner and then call owned() via vm.prank.)
For any address set as owner, when that owner calls owned() the contract's owner remains equal to that caller afterwards; the mutant breaks this by setting owner = address(0) inside owned().

Rule: calling any onlyOwner-guarded function must NOT change the owner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender in the modifier, so calling a guarded function by a different caller changes owner (violating the rule).
